items.bodyEn: Shōno was the final post town added to the Tōkaidō, in 1624, splitting the stage between Ishiyakushi and Kameyama. It stayed among the smallest: the 1843 survey counts fifteen inns and 855 residents. Its roadside specialty was yakigome, roasted rice that kept for days and needed no cooking, sold to travelers as trail food.
items.sourceNote: 東海道宿村大概帳 (1843): Shōno-juku, 15 hatago, 855 residents; est. 寛永元 (1624)

items.bodyEn: Hiroshige's 'Shōno: Driving Rain' is one of the two most celebrated designs of his Tōkaidō series, alongside the snow at Kanbara. Palanquin bearers and travelers under an umbrella struggle up a slope as a cloudburst slants across the sheet in fine grey lines and the bamboo bends. Nothing in the picture names Shōno; the weather is the subject.
items.sourceNote: Hiroshige, Tōkaidō gojūsan-tsugi (Hōeidō ed., 1833–34), 'Shōno: Hakuu' (白雨)

items.bodyEn: 白雨, 'white rain,' is the literary word in Hiroshige's title, read はくう. Dictionaries define it as a sudden shower that falls from a still-bright sky; the everyday word is 夕立. Japanese names its rains by season and mood: 時雨 for the passing showers of late autumn, 五月雨 for the long early-summer rains, 春雨 for soft spring drizzle.
items.sourceNote: Nihon Kokugo Daijiten (Shōgakukan), entry 白雨(はくう): 明るい空から降る雨、にわか雨

items.bodyEn: 〜がてら, 〜かたわら and 〜かたがた each pair one action with another, at different scales. 散歩がてら切手を買う folds a small errand into an outing. 会社員のかたわら小説を書く is a sideline carried on for years beside a main occupation. お礼かたがた伺います belongs to formal letters and visits. Use the first in chat, the second in a profile, the third in business mail.
items.ja: {散歩|さんぽ}がてら{切手|きって}を{買|か}う
items.kana: さんぽがてらきってをかう
